To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
CaM, but not PKC nor p 53, plays a critical role in the inhibition of DNA synthesis at early time points after exposure of human cells to ionizing radiation.
the CaM pathway is involved in radiation-induced inhibition of DNA replication in human cells and that the p53 pathway is not.

the inhibition of replicating DNA synthesis in human fibroblasts exposed to gamma rays is mediated by a signal transduction pathway that involves calmodulin but does not involve either protein kinase C or p53 protein.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the elucidation of molecular mechanisms which determine the cellular fate of DNA damaged by ionizing radiation.
elucidating how the cell cycle machinery is regulated in response to genotoxic stress and how such regulation is perturbed in A-T cells.
the elucidation of the biochemical events which underlie the cellular responses to ionizing radiation and which, when perturbed, may lead to the development of cancer and other diseases.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
CaM is not required for the G1/S cell cycle checkpoint in human cells.
the A-T syndrome results from a defect in the regulation of a signal transduction pathway that is required for normal cell cycle progression in response to DNA damage.
A-T cells have an abnormality of a CaM-dependent signal transduction system that is not p53 dependent and is not the same as PKC-dependent p53 activation.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the A-T defect in the G1/S arrest pathway is p53-independent and PKC-dependent, and that the RDS trait in A-T cells is PKC- and p53-independent and CaM-dependent.
A-T cells exhibit a radiation-induced defect in a p53- and PKC-dependent pathway controlling cell cycle progression and an RDS phenotype resulting from a CaM-dependent signalling mechanism.
the A-T phenotype is the result of multiple genetic defects, one or more of which is responsible for the RDS trait.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the G1/S arrest induced by gamma irradiation in human cells is a p53-independent process.
the RDS phenotype is not necessarily a reliable indicator of a defective p53-dependent G1/S checkpoint in A-T cells.
the RDS trait in A-T cells is not caused by a p53-dependent signalling anomaly.
